title: Cross-region QoS Routing Playbook: latency-aware, geo-pinning, and capacity steering
creator: Aisha Kaur
description: Playbook and implementation ticket for a unified cross-region routing policy that satisfies production SLOs while allowing geo-pinning for data locality and capacity-aware steering to avoid overload. This work defines algorithms, thresholds, circuit breaker behaviors, and a controllable rollout plan. Primary goals: (1) keep p99 latency under SLOs across regions, (2) ensure predictable failover behavior on region degradation without cascading overload, and (3) support per-tenant geo-pinning and priority shaping.
acceptance_criteria: Global routing policy deployed to canary customers in us-west-2 and eu-west-1
Automated fallback triggers when per-region p95 latency exceeds configured SLO for 30s
Circuit breaker opens for a region when CPU or GPU token/s exceeds threshold for 60s and a cooling period is enforced
Geo-pinning honored with TTL and override by capacity-aware steering when region capacity < 20% of demand
Load-shedding policy reduces best-effort requests by token-based probabilistic dropping and logs every dropped request with reason code
End-to-end tests (load + chaos) validating no more than 5% request loss for high-priority tenants during simulated regional outage
technical_decisions: Primary routing signal will be expected latency (p95) with secondary signal of regional available capacity (estimated tokens/s based on GPU allocation)
Use sticky geo-pinning via a RegionCookie+TTL (default 15 minutes) that can be overridden by CapacityOverride policy for safety
Circuit breaker state machine: CLOSED -> PROBATION (sampled traffic) -> OPEN (failover) with exponential backoff and adaptive recovery based on observed token drain
Load shedding algorithm: per-tenant priority buckets + token-weighted probabilistic drop (higher token requests drop with higher probability) to preserve p99 for priority tiers
Model variant fallback: route to smaller/quantized compatible model when capacity-constrained and when customer quality SLA allows
Telemetry: emit region_decision, decision_reason, region_capacity_pct, region_p95_ms, circuit_state, and shed_rate with 1s granularity to Grafana/Tempo
rollout_plan: Week 1: Feature flag behind routing.v2; enable canary in us-west-2 for internal traffic only
Week 2: Gradual ramp to 5% external traffic (non-priority tenants), run chaos test to throttle eu-west-1 network for 10m
Week 3: Enable geo-pinning TTL and capacity override for 10 enterprise tenants; monitor dashboards
Week 4: Expand to 25% traffic and run canary of model-fallback behavior; validate quality metrics
Full rollout conditioned on 2 consecutive weeks of metrics within thresholds
testing_plan: Synthetic load tests simulating skewed traffic (60% to eu-west-1) with step increases to trigger capacity steering
Chaos scenario: simulated region EBS IO saturation to validate circuit breaker and no-cascade failover
A/B tests for geo-pinning TTL values (5m, 15m, 60m) measuring user latency and session stickiness
Integration tests for token-weighted shedding using real prompt-size distributions from production traces
Regression tests ensuring routing decisions remain stable under transient latency spikes (<30s)
metrics_and_dashboards: SLO dashboard: p95/p99 latency per region and per-customer tier
Alerting: paging when circuit_state == OPEN for > 2m AND affected_traffic_pct > 10%
Shed logs: sink to BigQuery with schema (timestamp, tenant, reason_code, tokens, request_id)

notes: Trade-offs: heavy reliance on p95 introduces sensitivity to short-term noise; mitigated by probation sampling and hysteresis windows
Fallback to smaller model reduces latency but may impact hallucination rates; product to own mapping of tenant quality tolerance
We cannot rely solely on token counters from GPUs in all private deployments; add agent that reports tokens/s or fallback to CPU load metrics
Follow-up: add cost-aware steering that biases cheaper regions for non-sensitive workloads (future work)
